suggested_titles.academic: A Control-Theoretic Model of Divine Providence: PID Feedback, Stability, and the Sovereignty-Free Will Paradox
suggested_titles.provocative: God as PID Controller: How Control Theory Resolves the Sovereignty-Free Will Paradox

opening_analysis.diagnosis: The opening provides clear domain definitions and a mapping statement, but lacks a compelling hook. The problem (the sovereignty-free will paradox) is stated in the first paragraph but not framed as a tension that needs resolution. The reader gets context before motivation. A stronger opening would start with the paradox itself, then introduce control theory as the surprising resolution.

unresolved_tensions: The Calvinist/Arminian debate is formalized but not resolved — the paper acknowledges this as a feature, but some readers may expect a resolution.

missing_bridges: Between the 'Shared Structure' section and the 'Free Will Paradox Resolved' section, a brief transition explaining how the seven-part architecture leads to the paradox resolution would help.
redundant_passages: The 'What Is NOT Claimed' section partially repeats points made in the 'Free Will Paradox Resolved' section.
flow.suggested_reorder: Move the 'What Is NOT Claimed' section to immediately after the 'Shared Structure' section, before the 'Free Will Paradox Resolved' section, to preempt objections before the resolution is presented.

paragraph_function_map.main_point: This document maps control theory to Christian theology, specifically providence.
Domain A: Control theory concepts (PID, feedback, stability).
Domain B: Theological concepts (providence, sin, sanctification).
The mapping: providence is a PID controller with three temporal modes.
Mathematical form of the closed-loop transfer function.
PID controller equation.
Nyquist stability criterion.
Theological substitution into the control equations.
Providential PID controller with theological correlates for each mode.
Seven-part shared architecture between control theory and providence.
Setpoint-driven correction: error = sin.
Three temporal modes of correction: proportional, integral, derivative.
Negative feedback as stabilization (discipline).
Positive feedback as destabilization (giving over).
Disturbance rejection: evil attenuated, not eliminated.
Open-loop vs. closed-loop = deism vs. theism.
Controllability and observability: God can reach and know any state.
Free will paradox resolved: controller works through plant dynamics, not against them.
Stability question (apostasy) formalized via Nyquist criterion.
What is NOT claimed: six disclaimers to prevent overreach.
paragraph_function_map.problem: This section is defensive and interrupts the flow from the stability discussion to the tests. It could be moved earlier or integrated into the relevant sections.

rearrangement_suggestions: Move 'What Is NOT Claimed' section to immediately after the 'Shared Structure' section, before 'The Free Will Paradox Resolved'.
Add a transition paragraph between 'Shared Structure' and 'The Free Will Paradox Resolved' to explicitly connect the seven-part architecture to the paradox resolution.
Consider moving the 'Stability Question (Apostasy)' section to after the 'Free Will Paradox Resolved' section, as it is a separate application of the framework.
top_3_fixes: Strengthen the opening by leading with the sovereignty-free will paradox as a problem statement, then introducing control theory as the surprising resolution.
Move the 'What Is NOT Claimed' section earlier to preempt objections before the resolution is presented, improving flow and reader orientation.
Add a brief transition between the seven-part shared architecture and the free will paradox resolution to explicitly show how the architecture leads to the resolution.
